title: Unlocking Scientific Concepts: How Effective Are LLM-Generated Analogies for Student Understanding and Classroom Practice?
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '25)
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language model (LLM)-generated analogies can effectively support students’ understanding of scientific concepts and assist teachers in classroom practice. The authors focus on two educational scenarios: students using LLM-generated analogies without teacher intervention, and teachers integrating LLM-generated analogies into classroom teaching. The central questions are whether such analogies improve student understanding, what kinds of analogies teachers actually need, and how useful these analogies are when teachers can adapt them.

The intervention centers on GPT-4o-generated analogies for high school biology and physics concepts. In Study I, the authors ran a controlled in-class test in which one group of students used textbook explanations only, while another used textbook explanations plus LLM-generated analogies; outcomes included multiple-choice accuracy and self-confidence ratings, followed by student interviews. In Study II, the authors first interviewed teachers and senior students to identify requirements for classroom-useful analogies, then conducted a one-week classroom field study in which teachers used and modified generated analogies in one class while teaching another class as usual. Based on these findings, the authors also developed and evaluated a practical system to help teachers generate and refine analogies.

The study was conducted in a Chinese high school with first-year high school students, two teachers, and additional senior students consulted during interviews. Across the studies, the context was in-person school instruction in biology and physics classes. The classroom field study covered 12 lessons over one week, and the authors observed how teachers selected, refined, and used analogies, along with student feedback and homework-related performance impressions.

The main conclusions are that LLM-generated analogies can sometimes improve student understanding, particularly for biology concepts, but are unreliable for unsupervised student use because errors, omissions, and student over-reliance can undermine learning while increasing confidence. In classroom settings, teachers were able to refine and selectively use generated analogies in ways they found useful, reporting positive classroom feedback and perceived homework performance gains. Overall, the paper argues that LLM-generated analogies are more promising as teacher-facing supports for lesson preparation and guided classroom use than as standalone student self-learning tools.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods study with a controlled in-class comparison and classroom field study in K-12, but it is not a literacy study, uses small samples from one Chinese high school, and reports limited causal design detail and no standardized effect sizes. Evidence is therefore stronger than opinion but below well-designed RCT/QED standards.
impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests potentially beneficial but uneven effects: significant gains for some biology concept understanding and positive teacher-reported classroom use, alongside no clear physics benefit and risks of overconfidence or misunderstanding. Because impacts are mixed, domain-specific, and mostly lack effect sizes, overall impact is best classified as unclear/modest rather than clearly positive.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated analogy generation and teacher-facing refinement support for explaining high school biology and physics concepts in classroom instruction and student concept learning.

finding.finding_summary: This paper studies high-school students’ understanding of unfamiliar biology and physics concepts using LLM-generated analogies versus textbook explanation alone in a Chinese high school. In the controlled in-class test, biology accuracy showed a significant advantage for the analogy group (p=0.042), whereas no clear advantage appeared for physics; the authors also report mixed item-level patterns, including some lower performance when analogies omitted essential information or were incorrect. In the classroom field study, teachers reported positive classroom feedback and homework performance boosts when they refined and selectively used generated analogies, but these results were qualitative and no standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice concept question accuracy; item-level accuracy differences; teacher-reported classroom feedback and homework performance in biology/physics concept learning
finding.study_size: n=49 enrolled, 44 valid test papers in Study I; 50 students across 2 classes in Study II field study

finding.finding_summary: Students using LLM-generated analogies reported significantly higher confidence overall and by subject, including physics and biology, despite weak alignment between confidence and actual correctness. The paper reports negligible correlations between accuracy and confidence (absolute Kendall's tau <= 0.2), and interviews suggested over-reliance and overconfidence, especially when analogies were vivid but incomplete or erroneous.
finding.measure: 5-point self-confidence ratings; interview-reported perceptions of helpfulness, over-reliance, and classroom feedback
finding.study_size: n=44 valid test papers; 8 post-test student interviews; 2 teacher interviews plus classroom observations in field study

finding.finding_summary: Teachers in the field study and system evaluation found that LLM-generated analogies could be refined to teacher satisfaction and used to inspire additional analogies and teaching approaches during lesson preparation. The paper's evidence here is qualitative: teachers selected, modified, and reused generated analogies, and the authors subsequently built a practical system to support analogy generation and refinement, but no time-saved metric or workload reduction effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported usefulness for lesson preparation, analogy refinement, and ideation during classroom planning
finding.study_size: 2 teachers in pre-class interview and field study; 6 teachers in system evaluation
